06 · Brain Connectivity (resting-state fMRI) Classification¶

Can patterns of brain connectivity tell children with ADHD apart from typically developing children? This notebook trains classifiers on functional-connectivity matrices computed from resting-state fMRI.

This notebook
Data Nilearn's preprocessed ADHD-200 resting-state sample, 40 subjects (20 ADHD, 20 controls)
Atlases BASC multiscale (64 regions) and MSDL (39 probabilistic regions)
Connectivity correlation, partial correlation, tangent space
Models 7 classifiers × 3 connectivity kinds × 2 atlases
Validation repeated stratified 5-fold CV + a permutation test for significance

Pipeline: preprocessed fMRI → regional time series (atlas masking + confound regression + band-pass filtering) → region × region connectivity matrix → vectorised upper triangle → classifier.

1. Load the data¶

The preprocessed ADHD-200 sample distributed with Nilearn (40 subjects, ≈ 2.9 GB). neuroadhd.fmri.fetch_adhd_fmri downloads the same NITRC archives as nilearn.datasets.fetch_adhd, but in parallel and with resume support, into ~/nilearn_data (outside the project folder).

3. Extract regional time series¶

For each subject: average the signal within each region, regress out motion / physiological confounds, detrend, standardise and band-pass filter (0.01–0.1 Hz, TR = 2 s). Results are cached in data/processed/ so this slow step runs only once.

In [5]:
def extract(atlas_name):
    cache = DATA_PROCESSED / f"fmri_timeseries_{atlas_name}.npz"
    if cache.exists():
        z = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True); return list(z["ts"])
    common = dict(standardize="zscore_sample", detrend=True, low_pass=0.1, high_pass=0.01, t_r=2.0, memory="nilearn_cache", memory_level=1, verbose=0)
    masker = NiftiMapsMasker(msdl.maps, **common) if atlas_name == "msdl" else NiftiLabelsMasker(basc_img, **common)
    ts = [masker.fit_transform(f, confounds=c) for f, c in zip(adhd["func"], adhd["confounds"])]
    np.savez_compressed(cache, ts=np.array(ts, dtype=object))
    return ts

timeseries = {"msdl": extract("msdl"), "basc64": extract("basc64")}
for k, v in timeseries.items():
    print(f"{k}: {len(v)} subjects, time series shape of subject 0 = {v[0].shape}")

msdl: 40 subjects, time series shape of subject 0 = (176, 39)

5. Classification¶

Features: the vectorised upper triangle of each connectivity matrix (741 features for MSDL, 2,016 for BASC-64) for only 40 subjects, a severe p ≫ n problem. The connectivity transform (notably tangent, which learns a group-mean reference) is fitted inside each training fold to avoid leakage. Validation: 5-fold stratified CV repeated 10 times (50 fits per configuration).

In [9]:
classifiers = {
    "Linear SVM": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LinearSVC(C=0.01, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=20000))]),
    "Logistic (L2)": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression(C=0.01, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=5000))]),
    "Ridge": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", RidgeClassifier(alpha=100, class_weight="balanced"))]),
    "PCA + SVM (RBF)": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("pca", PCA(n_components=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)), ("clf", SVC(class_weight="balanced"))]),
    "KNN": Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))]),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
}
rskf = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

def score_of(clf, X):
    return clf.decision_function(X) if hasattr(clf, "decision_function") else clf.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

rows = []
for atlas, ts_list in timeseries.items():
    ts_arr = np.array(ts_list, dtype=object)
    for kind in kinds:
        res = {n: {"acc": [], "f1": [], "auc": []} for n in classifiers}
        for tr, te in rskf.split(np.zeros(len(y)), y):
            cm = ConnectivityMeasure(kind=kind, vectorize=True, discard_diagonal=True)
            Xtr = cm.fit_transform(list(ts_arr[tr])); Xte = cm.transform(list(ts_arr[te]))
            for n, clf in classifiers.items():
                m = clone(clf).fit(Xtr, y[tr]); pred = m.predict(Xte)
                res[n]["acc"].append(accuracy_score(y[te], pred)); res[n]["f1"].append(f1_score(y[te], pred, zero_division=0))
                res[n]["auc"].append(roc_auc_score(y[te], score_of(m, Xte)))
        for n, r in res.items():
            rows.append({"atlas": atlas, "connectivity": kind, "model": n, "accuracy": np.mean(r["acc"]), "accuracy_sd": np.std(r["acc"]),
                         "f1": np.mean(r["f1"]), "roc_auc": np.mean(r["auc"])})
fmri_res = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("accuracy", ascending=False)
fmri_res.round(3).head(15)

    ax.text(max(y.mean(), 1 - y.mean()) + 0.005, len(models_order) - 0.4, "majority-class\nbaseline", fontsize=8.5, color=INK_2, va="top")
    ax.set_yticks(yy, models_order); ax.set_xlim(0.3, 0.85); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

6. Is the best result better than chance? (permutation test)¶

With 40 subjects, an accuracy of 0.65 can happen by luck. We re-run the best configuration 500 times with shuffled labels to build the null distribution.

In [11]:
best = fmri_res.iloc[0]
print("Best configuration:", dict(best[["atlas", "connectivity", "model", "accuracy", "roc_auc"]]))
Xbest = ConnectivityMeasure(kind=best.connectivity, vectorize=True, discard_diagonal=True).fit_transform(timeseries[best.atlas])
# (correlation / partial correlation are per-subject transforms, so pre-computing them is leakage-free; tangent is approximated here)
score, perm_scores, pval = permutation_test_score(clone(classifiers[best.model]), Xbest, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
                                                  n_permutations=500, scoring="accuracy", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.hist(perm_scores, bins=25, color=MUTED, alpha=0.7, edgecolor=SURFACE, label="shuffled labels (null)")
ax.axvline(score, color=ADHD_COLOR, lw=2.5, label=f"true labels: {score:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("CV accuracy"); ax.set_ylabel("permutations"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title(f"Permutation test · {best.model}, {best.connectivity}, {best.atlas.upper()} · p = {pval:.3f}")
savefig(fig, "06_permutation_test"); plt.show()

Best configuration: {'atlas': 'msdl', 'connectivity': 'correlation', 'model': 'PCA + SVM (RBF)', 'accuracy': np.float64(0.5575), 'roc_auc': np.float64(0.62625)}

7. Confusion matrices (out-of-fold predictions, best configuration per model family)¶

In [12]:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
show = ["Linear SVM", "Random Forest", "Decision Tree"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.4))
cm_out = {}
for ax, n in zip(axes, show):
    b = fmri_res[fmri_res.model == n].iloc[0]
    Xb = ConnectivityMeasure(kind=b.connectivity, vectorize=True, discard_diagonal=True).fit_transform(timeseries[b.atlas])
    pred = cross_val_predict(clone(classifiers[n]), Xb, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))
    cm = confusion_matrix(y, pred); cm_out[n] = cm.tolist(); pct = cm / cm.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    ax.imshow(pct, cmap=SEQ_BLUE, vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{cm[i, j]}\n{pct[i, j]:.0%}", ha="center", va="center", color="white" if pct[i, j] > 0.55 else INK, fontsize=12, fontweight="semibold")
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["Control", "ADHD"]); ax.set_yticks([0, 1], ["Control", "ADHD"]); ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("true"); ax.set_title(f"{n}\n{b.atlas.upper()} · {b.connectivity}", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "06_fmri_confusion"); plt.show()

Conclusions¶

Results in numbers

  • Best of 42 configurations: PCA + SVM (RBF) on MSDL correlation, accuracy 0.56, ROC-AUC 0.63 (repeated 5-fold CV). Most configurations sit between 0.45 and 0.55, around the 0.50 chance level.
  • Permutation test: accuracy 0.60 vs. a null mean of 0.50, p = 0.11, so the result is not significantly better than chance.
  • Picking the best of 42 settings is itself optimistic (selection bias), so the true expected accuracy is closer to chance than the top number suggests.

Interpretation

  • Connectivity matrices show subtle, diffuse group differences (right-hand matrix above), with no single "ADHD connection".
  • With hundreds to thousands of connectivity features and only 40 subjects, single train/test splits swing widely (fold-level SD ≈ 0.15), so results from small samples should be read with caution. Large-sample studies (e.g. the full ADHD-200 competition) reached only ~60–65 % accuracy from imaging.
  • Practical lesson: in this project, questionnaire-based and demographic models (notebooks 04–05) are far more predictive than imaging from a small sample.
